passages.passage_text:
Marketing, which is sometimes called distribution, includes all the business activities connected with the movement of goods and services from producers to consumers. Marketing consists of both physical activities such as transporting, storing and selling goods, and a series of decisions related to any part of the process of moving goods from the producer to the consumer. Marketing operations include product planning, buying, storage, pricing, promotion, selling, credit, and marketing research.

The ability to recognise future trends is as important as knowing the present conditions in marketing. Producers must know why consumers buy, where and for what purpose. Through market research, the producer tries to predict what the customer will want and, through advertising, attempts to influence what the customer will buy.

In most countries, manufacturers obviously spend a lot of money on advertising their goods. We cannot walk down the street, watch television or read a newspaper without being 'attacked' by advertisements. Doubtless, many people think that too much money is spent on advertising. "Wouldn't it be better," they say, "to spend all this advertising money on improving the product or service, or on projects to help poor people?" Advertising, however, is essential for a manufacturer's survival. It is vital to keep the name of the product in front of the public. Otherwise, sales will fall. Another manufacturer of the same kind of product may continue advertising and his name will be the one that people remember when they go shopping. And his sales will increase.

Some people will then almost certainly say, "But why should two or more companies produce the same things? Surely, it is more economical for each company to produce a different product. Then, there would be little or no need for any advertising." But there is a sensible economic answer to this argument as well. Competition between companies is vital because it helps to improve the quality of the product and to keep prices down. The result is a better and cheaper product for the public. Since competition is essential, advertising is vital.

In most countries, manufacturers obviously spend a lot of money on advertising their goods. We cannot walk down the street, watch television or read a newspaper without being 'attacked' by advertisements. Doubtless, many people think that too much money is spent on advertising. "Wouldn't it be better," they say, "to spend all this advertising money on improving the product or service, or on projects to help poor people?" Advertising, however, is essential for a manufacturer's survival. It is vital to keep the name of the product in front of the public. Otherwise, sales will fall. Another manufacturer of the same kind of product may continue advertising and his name will be the one that people remember when they go shopping. And his sales will increase.

Some people will then almost certainly say, "But why should two or more companies produce the same things? Surely, it is more economical for each company to produce a different product. Then, there would be little or no need for any advertising." But there is a sensible economic answer to this argument as well. Competition between companies is vital because it helps to improve the quality of the product and to keep prices down. The result is a better and cheaper product for the public. Since competition is essential, advertising is vital.

task2.model_answer:
Many consumers complain that companies spend excessive sums on advertising instead of lowering prices or improving products. While this criticism is understandable when advertisements feel intrusive, advertising plays an essential role in a healthy, competitive market.

On the one hand, huge marketing budgets can raise business costs, and aggressive campaigns sometimes persuade people to buy unnecessary items. In monopolies where only one company sells a product, heavy advertising would indeed bring little benefit to consumers.

On the other hand, in competitive industries, advertising helps new and existing businesses inform customers about better features or lower prices. Without visibility, even a high-quality product could fail simply because shoppers do not know it exists. As the passage explains, competition pushes firms to improve quality and keep prices affordable, and advertising keeps that competition alive. Therefore, while misleading claims should be regulated, advertising itself benefits the public by supporting choice, innovation, and competitive pricing.

Pazarlama, hem malların taşınması, depolanması ve satılması gibi fiziksel faaliyetlerden hem de malları üreticiden tüketiciye taşıma sürecinin herhangi bir bölümüyle ilgili bir dizi karardan oluşur. Pazarlama faaliyetleri ürün planlama, satın alma, depolama, fiyatlandırma, tanıtım, satış, kredi ve pazarlama araştırmasını kapsar.

Pazarlamada gelecekteki eğilimleri öngörebilme yeteneği, mevcut koşulları bilmek kadar önemlidir. Üreticiler tüketicilerin neden, nereden ve hangi amaçla satın aldıklarını bilmelidir. Üretici, pazar araştırması yoluyla müşterinin ne isteyeceğini tahmin etmeye çalışır ve reklam yoluyla da müşterinin ne satın alacağını etkilemeye uğraşır.

"Tüm bu reklam parasını ürünü ya da hizmeti geliştirmeye veya yoksul insanlara yardım eden projelere harcamak daha iyi olmaz mıydı?" derler. passages.passage_text:
It is widely believed that the world's population has exploded because of the improvements in medical science, which has naturally led to improved standards of public health. Infant mortality has been greatly reduced and the average length of life has been extended on a great scale.

Demographers, or population statisticians, are less alarmed by the absolute rise in the world population figures than by the increase in the rate of growth. They estimate that it will take only about 30 years for the world population to double. Pessimists expect this soaring growth to continue until the limits of food, space and natural resources are forced.

It is not easy to find solutions to problems caused by population growth. In fact, effective action is lacking because of our inability to decide exactly where the problems lie. For example, many millions of people do not have enough to eat, but at the same time we could argue that the world is not over-populated in relation to its food supply at the present time. The total cultivable land is more than 15 billion acres. Using modern agricultural methods, we could produce more than enough food for the present population of about 5 billion.

It appears, then, that the world's population could be almost three times as large before there is a serious shortage of food. But it is unlikely that all the cultivable land would be used for food production. If this were done, there would not be any land left to meet man's increasing demand for houses, factories, airports, roads and other facilities.

task2.model_answer:
Rapid population growth places pressure not only on food production but also on living space and infrastructure. As the passage points out, the Earth theoretically has enough cultivable land to feed far more than 5 billion people. However, feeding a larger population is not simply an agricultural challenge. People also require homes, factories, roads, and airports, all of which compete for the same limited land.

To balance these competing needs, governments should invest in sustainable urban planning and higher-yield farming. Building denser, well-planned cities can reduce urban sprawl and preserve fertile soil for agriculture. At the same time, improving food distribution systems is just as important as increasing total harvests, since millions already suffer from hunger even when global food supplies are sufficient. By combining smarter land use with fairer distribution, societies can support growing populations without exhausting natural resources.

Demograflar, yani nüfus istatistikçileri, dünya nüfus rakamlarındaki mutlak artıştan ziyade büyüme hızındaki artıştan endişe duymaktadır. Kötümserler, bu hızla yükselen artışın gıda, yaşam alanı ve doğal kaynakların sınırları zorlanana kadar devam etmesini beklemektedir.

Nüfus artışının yol açtığı sorunlara çözüm bulmak kolay değildir. Aslında sorunların tam olarak nerede yattığına karar veremememiz nedeniyle etkili adımlar atılamamaktadır. Örneğin, milyonlarca insanın yiyecek yeterli gıdası yoktur; ancak aynı zamanda dünyanın şu anda gıda arzına kıyasla aşırı kalabalık olmadığını da savunabiliriz. Toplam ekilebilir arazi 15 milyar akreden fazladır. Modern tarım yöntemlerini kullanarak yaklaşık 5 milyarlık mevcut nüfus için fazlasıyla yeterli gıda üretebiliriz.

Öyleyse ciddi bir gıda kıtlığı yaşanmadan önce dünya nüfusunun neredeyse üç katına çıkabileceği görülmektedir. Ancak tüm ekilebilir arazinin gıda üretimi için kullanılması pek olası değildir. Eğer bu yapılsaydı, insanın ev, fabrika, havalimanı, yol ve diğer tesislere yönelik artan talebini karşılayacak hiç arazi kalmazdı.

passages.passage_text:
A laser is a very strong beam of light which is very different from ordinary light. Today, doctors use lasers in some eye operations. They use them when operating on a patient who has a detached (i.e. separated) retina. The retina is the inner back part of the eye, the part that senses light. Light from an object must strike the retina for seeing to occur.

In the past, a detached retina caused blindness in the eye. Now, the laser makes delicate eye operations possible, and a detached retina no longer means the loss of sight. By carefully directing this super light beam, the doctor can weld the retina to the rest of the eye again. The welding of the retina takes less than a thousandth of a second and is done without anesthesia. Anesthetizing the patient is not necessary, because the patient feels no pain.

Doctors also want to use lasers in operations on people who have heart diseases. In the United States and Canada alone, more than 1.5 million people suffer from heart diseases every year. Most of these are related to the flow of blood through the coronary arteries, which supply the majority of the blood to the heart. People who have a heart disease have a high amount of cholesterol in their blood. Cholesterol builds up fatty deposits called 'plaques' on the inner walls of the arteries. As the plaques get bigger, the opening of the artery gets smaller. When it is completely closed, blood stops flowing and the heart attack occurs.

Some doctors are planning to use lasers to destroy these fatty deposits in the near future. More studies are needed, but some doctors feel this plan will be beneficial for heart patients. At present, though, lasers have many other uses in hospitals; they are used in sterilizing instruments, stopping bleeding and removing birthmarks.

task2.model_answer:
Modern medical technology has transformed the way doctors diagnose and treat serious illnesses. As shown in the passage, tools like lasers allow surgeons to perform delicate eye operations quickly and painlessly, saving patients from permanent blindness. passages.passage_text:
By the year 2000, the world population is expected to be about 7,000 million. This great increase in the world population, or 'demographic explosion' as it has been called, will cause many problems: shortage of housing, shortage of facilities and psychological stress. But the biggest problem of all will be the shortage of food. In 1973, in West and Central Africa, there were serious deficiencies of basic foods such as corn, rice, milk and meat. This was partly because of natural disasters such as drought (not enough rain) and floods, that is, too much rain, but basically it was because of a real shortage of these foods. Everywhere in the world, the prices of basic foods rose and it became impossible for many people to buy enough of them. Nutritional experts estimated that half the world's population was under-nourished and that millions were near starvation. And in 1973, the population of the world was only half of what it may be in the year 2000!

Agricultural experts are trying to increase the output of food in the world without great increase in price. They are working on projects for breeding plants and animals which are bigger, grow faster and are resistant to diseases. In India, for example, new strains of rice have been developed, which has greatly increased yields. In Mexico, excellent new varieties of wheat have been produced by Dr. Norman E. Borlaug, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970 for his work.

However, increasing yields in this way may be expensive, and may require large quantities of fertiliser to 'feed' the land. If the population continues to grow, more and more agricultural land will be needed for housing. For many years now, experts have been experimenting with techniques of cultivating plants by using mixtures of chemical compounds and water only. This is called 'hydroponics', and if it becomes economical, vegetables and fruit could be produced in factories instead of fields. In addition, agricultural scientists have been cross-breeding livestock - cattle, pigs, chickens, etc. - to produce better animals.

Mechanisation is another way of producing more food. Machines can do work faster, more efficiently and more cheaply than man and they are being used in industrialised countries to do almost all farming jobs.

One of the best hopes scientists have for solving the food crisis is to find new sources of food, especially protein. Experimental food is now being produced from petroleum, from seaweed and from other surprising raw materials.

task1.model_answer: Rapid global population growth, often called a demographic explosion, threatens to cause severe shortages of housing, facilities, and especially food. In 1973, droughts, floods, and overall supply shortages left millions of people under-nourished, even though the population then was half of its projected 2000 level. To prevent future crises without raising prices sharply, experts are developing faster-growing, disease-resistant crops like high-yield rice in India and wheat in Mexico, cross-breeding livestock, and mechanising farm work. Scientists are also exploring hydroponics to grow produce without farmland and creating experimental protein-rich foods from unconventional materials such as seaweed and petroleum.
task1.prompt: Summarize the main causes of the global food problem and the solutions scientists and agricultural experts are developing, as described in the passage.
task1.title: Summarizing the Global Food Challenge

task2.model_answer: In my opinion, traditional agriculture alone will not be enough to feed a rapidly growing global population, so society must invest in modern scientific farming techniques. First, arable land is limited, and expanding cities continuously reduce the space available for conventional crops. Methods such as hydroponics offer a practical way to grow fresh fruit and vegetables inside urban factories while using water efficiently. Second, climate unpredictability, including severe droughts and floods, frequently damages traditional harvests. Developing disease-resistant and weather-tolerant plant varieties helps protect food supplies against sudden shortages. Although some people worry about the cost of fertilisers, machinery, or experimental protein sources, ongoing research can make these technologies safer and more affordable over time. Ultimately, combining sustainable traditional farming with scientific innovation is the most reliable way to prevent widespread hunger.
task2.prompt: Do you think modern scientific techniques like hydroponics and experimental food are necessary to feed the growing world population, or should societies focus on traditional farming? Give reasons to support your view.
task2.title: Opinion Essay: Science vs. Traditional Farming

passages.passage_text:
Many years ago, when most people got their water directly from wells under the ground, they were sometimes annoyed by a dark liquid which came out of the ground and contaminated the water. It smelled bad and was extremely dirty. Some people discovered that it was good for caulking boats - it prevented water from getting in through the cracks in the wood. Others found it was a good medicine for the stomach. However, most people didn't like it. Today, we have a rather different opinion on this substance known as crude oil.

In 1855, a young teacher at Yale University, Benjamin Silliman, became interested in crude oil. He soon found that it could be used as a fuel for heating and lighting. After the first oil well started production, the age of oil was just around the corner. Today, J. P. Getty and Howard Hughes, two of the richest men in the world, both have fortunes based on oil - the former on the Standard Oil Co. and the latter on a highly efficient oil-drilling bit.

The first oil from the sea was produced some decades ago by the off-shore drilling rigs in Maracaibo Bay, Venezuela. There, the water is shallow and the oil is very near the surface. The tropical forest comes right down to the water's edge, and today it seems to continue into the sea. The oil is quite easy to get out in this area, but men are now also drilling in more difficult areas like the cold, deep North Sea between Great Britain and Norway.

The petroleum which comes out of the ground cannot really be used for anything. It must first be refined. Refineries are huge 'factories' where crude oil is separated into 'fractions', which are commonly known as gasoline, kerosene, diesel oil, lubricating oil and fuel oil. Then, these fractions must be distributed by pipeline or tanker to the final distributors, such as petrol stations, which sell them to the users.

Every person in industrial societies depends on crude oil. Its fractions provide fuel for electricity generators, power for vehicles, heat for homes and materials for clothing. In the future, we may use some of its fractions to produce food.

The question is: how long will the world's reserves of crude oil last? We use more and more oil every year. Crude oil is a non-renewable resource and one day it will probably run out. Many things will be different when this happens, but the most interesting and important question is what alternative sources of energy will be successfully developed.

passages.tts_script:

Many years ago, when most people got their water directly from wells under the ground, they were sometimes annoyed by a dark liquid which came out of the ground and contaminated the water. It smelled bad and was extremely dirty. Some people discovered that it was good for caulking boats, because it prevented water from getting in through the cracks in the wood. Others found it was a good medicine for the stomach. However, most people didn't like it. Today, we have a rather different opinion on this substance known as crude oil.

In 1855, a young teacher at Yale University, Benjamin Silliman, became interested in crude oil. He soon found that it could be used as a fuel for heating and lighting. After the first oil well started production, the age of oil was just around the corner. Today, J. P. Getty and Howard Hughes, two of the richest men in the world, both have fortunes based on oil, the former on the Standard Oil Company and the latter on a highly efficient oil-drilling bit.

The first oil from the sea was produced some decades ago by the off-shore drilling rigs in Maracaibo Bay, Venezuela. There, the water is shallow and the oil is very near the surface. The tropical forest comes right down to the water's edge, and today it seems to continue into the sea. The oil is quite easy to get out in this area, but men are now also drilling in more difficult areas like the cold, deep North Sea between Great Britain and Norway.

The petroleum which comes out of the ground cannot really be used for anything. It must first be refined. Refineries are huge factories where crude oil is separated into fractions, which are commonly known as gasoline, kerosene, diesel oil, lubricating oil and fuel oil. Then, these fractions must be distributed by pipeline or tanker to the final distributors, such as petrol stations, which sell them to the users.

Every person in industrial societies depends on crude oil. Its fractions provide fuel for electricity generators, power for vehicles, heat for homes and materials for clothing. In the future, we may use some of its fractions to produce food.

The question is: how long will the world's reserves of crude oil last? We use more and more oil every year. Crude oil is a non-renewable resource and one day it will probably run out. Many things will be different when this happens, but the most interesting and important question is what alternative sources of energy will be successfully developed.

task1.model_answer: Long ago, crude oil was considered an unpleasant liquid that polluted water wells, though a few people used it for caulking boats or treating stomach problems. Its real value became clear in 1855 when Benjamin Silliman discovered it could be used for heating and lighting, launching the modern oil industry. Today, offshore rigs extract oil from shallow waters like Maracaibo Bay as well as harsher regions like the North Sea. Because raw petroleum cannot be used directly, refineries separate it into fractions such as gasoline, kerosene, and diesel oil. Industrial societies rely heavily on these products for electricity, transport, heating, and clothing, yet this non-renewable resource will eventually run out.
task1.prompt: Summarize how people's view and use of crude oil have changed from the past to modern times, including how it is processed and why its future is uncertain.
task1.title: Summarizing the History and Future of Crude Oil

task2.model_answer: Because crude oil is a non-renewable resource that industrial societies depend on heavily, governments should invest urgently in alternative sources of energy. First, global oil consumption rises every year, meaning existing reserves will eventually be depleted. Waiting until oil runs out would cause severe economic disruption, affecting everything from public transport to home heating and electricity generation. Developing solar, wind, and hydroelectric power early allows countries to transition smoothly without sudden energy crises. Second, burning oil fractions contributes to air pollution and environmental damage, whereas clean energy alternatives reduce harmful emissions. Even though building renewable energy infrastructure requires high initial investment and technological research, the long-term benefits are far greater. By diversifying their energy sources now, nations can protect both their economies and the environment for future generations.

passages.tts_script_tr:
Ham Petrol.

Uzun yıllar önce, çoğu insan suyunu doğrudan yer altındaki kuyulardan aldığında, bazen yerden çıkan ve suyu kirleten koyu renkli bir sıvıdan rahatsız olurlardı. Kötü kokuyordu ve son derece kirliydi. Bazı insanlar bunun tekneleri kalafatlamak için iyi olduğunu keşfetti, çünkü ahşaptaki çatlaklardan su girmesini önlüyordu. Diğerleri ise mide için iyi bir ilaç olduğunu buldu. Ancak çoğu insan bundan hoşlanmıyordu. Bugün ise ham petrol olarak bilinen bu madde hakkında oldukça farklı bir görüşe sahibiz.

1855 yılında, Yale Üniversitesi'nde genç bir öğretmen olan Benjamin Silliman ham petrole ilgi duymaya başladı. Kısa süre içinde bunun ısınma ve aydınlatma için yakıt olarak kullanılabileceğini keşfetti. İlk petrol kuyusunun üretime başlamasının ardından petrol çağı artık çok yakındı. Bugün dünyanın en zengin insanlarından ikisi olan J. P. Getty ve Howard Hughes'un servetleri petrole dayanmaktadır; ilki Standard Oil Company'ye, ikincisi ise son derece verimli bir petrol sondaj matkabına dayanmaktadır.

Denizden ilk petrol birkaç on yıl önce Venezuela'daki Maracaibo Körfezi'nde bulunan açık deniz sondaj platformları tarafından çıkarıldı. Orada su sığdır ve petrol yüzeye çok yakındır. Tropikal orman tam suyun kenarına kadar uzanır ve bugün denizin içine doğru devam ediyormuş gibi görünür. Bu bölgede petrolü çıkarmak oldukça kolaydır, ancak insanlar artık Büyük Britanya ile Norveç arasındaki soğuk ve derin Kuzey Denizi gibi daha zorlu alanlarda da sondaj yapmaktadır.

Yerden çıkan petrol aslında doğrudan hiçbir şey için kullanılamaz. Önce rafine edilmesi gerekir. Rafineriler, ham petrolün yaygın olarak benzin, gaz yağı, dizel yakıt, yağlama yağı ve akaryakıt olarak bilinen fraksiyonlara ayrıldığı devasa fabrikalardır. Ardından bu fraksiyonlar, boru hattı veya tankerlerle benzin istasyonları gibi son dağıtıcılara ulaştırılmalı ve onlar tarafından kullanıcılara satılmalıdır.

Sanayi toplumlarındaki her insan ham petrole bağımlıdır. Petrolün fraksiyonları elektrik jeneratörleri için yakıt, araçlar için güç, evler için ısı ve giysiler için malzeme sağlar. Gelecekte, gıda üretmek için de bazı fraksiyonlarını kullanabiliriz.

Soru şu: Dünyanın ham petrol rezervleri ne kadar süre dayanacak? Her yıl giderek daha fazla petrol kullanıyoruz. Ham petrol yenilenemeyen bir kaynaktır ve bir gün muhtemelen tükenecektir. Bu gerçekleştiğinde pek çok şey farklı olacaktır, ancak en ilginç ve önemli soru hangi alternatif enerji kaynaklarının başarıyla geliştirileceğidir.

passages.passage_text:
The voice on the other end of the line was insistent. "We need that contract and we need it badly. You know how bad our financial situation is at the moment - this contract could be the difference between life and death for us. I don't care how you do it, but you must get that contract." Tony Adamson put down the phone and sighed. He felt that his boss in London just did not understand how difficult things were for him in Zalesia. He knew that in reality his company had very little chance of getting the contract, which was to supply a large amount of furniture and other equipment to the new University of Zalesia. There were too many other companies interested - bigger companies that he knew would be able to offer equal quality, and probably a much better price.

Adamson's only hope was that he might be able to get the contract through a personal contact that he had inside the Ministry. During his three years as Eduquip's Marketing Manager in the area, he had developed a strong personal friendship with Elua Tahi, an official in the Ministry who Adamson knew was on the committee that was dealing with the University project. It wasn't unusual for contracts in Zalesia to be given because of friendship rather than price. Maybe, Adamson thought, he had more chance than he thought.

The next day, Adamson went to see Tahi in his office. For the first half hour they chatted about personal topics, and then Adamson introduced the subject of the contract. "This contract is important to you, isn't it?" said Tahi. Adamson nodded. "Yes, and we need your support on the committee. You've bought equipment from Eduquip before, for the Zalesian schools. You know our quality is good, and our delivery dates are reliable. Why change to a supplier you don't know, who might cause you problems?"

"Yes," said Tahi. "Well, I'll see what I can do. But there are a lot of other companies interested too, of course. Oh, by the way, while you're here, there's a favour that I wanted to ask you." "Sure," said Adamson. "Anything I can do." "My wife has to have an operation, and she wants to have it in England. Obviously it's going to be expensive, and you know our government's rules about taking money out of the country. She really needs $2,000 waiting for her when she arrives in England. There's no way it could be organised, I suppose?"

For a moment Adamson was too surprised to speak. Tahi was clearly asking for a bribe. There was really no reason for him to be surprised - he knew that bribery was normal business practice in Zalesia, even though there were strict laws against it. Any company representative caught offering bribes to government officials risked up to five years' imprisonment. But he had always previously thought that Tahi was different from the majority of Zalesian officials - that was why he had become so friendly with him. So far in Zalesia, Adamson had managed never to do anything that could be considered more than a small favour in order to win a contract. He did not believe in bribery, and certainly had no wish to spend any time in a Zalesian jail.

Tahi obviously noticed Adamson's confusion. "Don't worry," he said. "If it's a problem for you, there are others I can ask." His meaning was clear. If Eduquip didn't pay the bribe, another company would.

passages.title: A Familiar Story
passages.tts_script:
A Familiar Story.

The voice on the other end of the line was insistent. "We need that contract and we need it badly. You know how bad our financial situation is at the moment - this contract could be the difference between life and death for us. I don't care how you do it, but you must get that contract." Tony Adamson put down the phone and sighed. He felt that his boss in London just did not understand how difficult things were for him in Zalesia. He knew that in reality his company had very little chance of getting the contract, which was to supply a large amount of furniture and other equipment to the new University of Zalesia. There were too many other companies interested - bigger companies that he knew would be able to offer equal quality, and probably a much better price.

Adamson's only hope was that he might be able to get the contract through a personal contact that he had inside the Ministry. During his three years as Eduquip's Marketing Manager in the area, he had developed a strong personal friendship with Elua Tahi, an official in the Ministry who Adamson knew was on the committee that was dealing with the University project. It wasn't unusual for contracts in Zalesia to be given because of friendship rather than price. Maybe, Adamson thought, he had more chance than he thought.

The next day, Adamson went to see Tahi in his office. For the first half hour they chatted about personal topics, and then Adamson introduced the subject of the contract. "This contract is important to you, isn't it?" said Tahi. Adamson nodded. "Yes, and we need your support on the committee. You've bought equipment from Eduquip before, for the Zalesian schools. You know our quality is good, and our delivery dates are reliable. Why change to a supplier you don't know, who might cause you problems?"

"Yes," said Tahi. "Well, I'll see what I can do. But there are a lot of other companies interested too, of course. Oh, by the way, while you're here, there's a favour that I wanted to ask you." "Sure," said Adamson. "Anything I can do." "My wife has to have an operation, and she wants to have it in England. Obviously it's going to be expensive, and you know our government's rules about taking money out of the country. She really needs two thousand dollars waiting for her when she arrives in England. There's no way it could be organised, I suppose?"

For a moment Adamson was too surprised to speak. Tahi was clearly asking for a bribe. There was really no reason for him to be surprised - he knew that bribery was normal business practice in Zalesia, even though there were strict laws against it. Any company representative caught offering bribes to government officials risked up to five years' imprisonment. But he had always previously thought that Tahi was different from the majority of Zalesian officials - that was why he had become so friendly with him. So far in Zalesia, Adamson had managed never to do anything that could be considered more than a small favour in order to win a contract. He did not believe in bribery, and certainly had no wish to spend any time in a Zalesian jail.

Tahi obviously noticed Adamson's confusion. "Don't worry," he said. "If it's a problem for you, there are others I can ask." His meaning was clear. If Eduquip didn't pay the bribe, another company would.

task2.model_answer:
In international business, companies often operate in countries where informal payments or bribes are treated as normal practice. However, businesses should refuse to pay bribes even when losing a major contract threatens their financial survival.

First, bribery destroys fair competition and lowers overall standards. When contracts are awarded to whichever firm pays an official rather than the one offering the best quality and price, public institutions such as schools and universities receive poorer value. Second, participating in corruption exposes employees and companies to severe legal and reputational risks. As Tony's story shows, a representative caught offering a bribe may face years in prison, and a company's reputation can be permanently damaged once such practices come to light.

Although turning down a lucrative deal can cause short-term hardship, firms should compete through transparent pricing, reliable delivery, and strong service. Upholding ethical standards protects both employees and long-term business integrity.

Zalesia'da sözleşmelerin fiyattan ziyade dostluk sayesinde verilmesi alışılmadık bir durum değildi. Adamson, belki de düşündüğünden daha fazla şansı olduğunu aklından geçirdi.

Adamson başıyla onayladı. "Evet ve komitede sizin desteğinize ihtiyacımız var. Daha önce Zalesia okulları için Eduquip'ten ekipman satın almıştınız. "Evet," dedi Tahi. "Şey, elimden geleni yapmaya çalışacağım. Ama tabii ilgilenen pek çok başka şirket de var. Ha, bu arada, hazır buradayken senden isteyeceğim bir iyilik vardı." "Elbette," dedi Adamson. "Elimden gelen bir şeyse." "Eşimin bir ameliyat olması gerekiyor ve bunu İngiltere'de yaptırmak istiyor. Doğal olarak pahalıya mal olacak ve hükümetimizin yurt dışına para çıkarma konusundaki kurallarını biliyorsun. İngiltere'ye vardığında orada kendisini bekleyen iki bin dolara gerçekten ihtiyacı var. Sanırım bunu ayarlamanın bir yolu yoktur, değil mi?"

Adamson bir an şaşkınlıktan konuşamadı. Tahi açıkça rüşvet istiyordu. Aslında şaşırması için hiçbir neden yoktu; buna karşı katı yasalar olmasına rağmen Zalesia'da rüşvetin olağan bir iş uygulaması olduğunu biliyordu. Devlet görevlilerine rüşvet teklif ederken yakalanan herhangi bir şirket temsilcisi beş yıla kadar hapis cezası riskiyle karşı karşıya kalıyordu. Ancak daha önce Tahi'nin Zalesialı görevlilerin çoğunluğundan farklı olduğunu düşünmüştü; onunla bu kadar samimi olmasının nedeni de buydu. Rüşvete inanmıyordu ve kesinlikle bir Zalesia hapishanesinde vakit geçirmek gibi bir niyeti yoktu.

Tahi, Adamson'ın şaşkınlığını açıkça fark etmişti. "Endişelenme," dedi. "Senin için bir sorun teşkil ediyorsa, sorabileceğim başkaları var." Ne demek istediği açıktı. Eğer Eduquip rüşveti ödemezse, başka bir şirket ödeyecekti.

passages.passage_text:
The first moving pictures were developed in the 1890's by W.K.L. Dickson, an Englishman working in the USA. He called his system the Kinetoscope. It wasn't the cinema as we know it at all. The pictures were very small and only one person at a time could watch. The earliest Kinetoscope used sound separately recorded on a phonograph (an ancestor of the gramophone and record player). But there were many problems involved in getting the picture and sound together, that is, synchronising. As a result, the Kinetoscope was popularised in its silent form. The same principle was developed by the Frenchmen, Auguste and Louis Lumiere. They called their system the Cinematographe and, between 1895 and 1900, succeeded in exporting it to other parts of Europe, to India, Australia and Japan. The Cinematographe used a large screen, but the films were still very short - only about a minute long. Like the popularised Kinetoscope, it was a silent system.

The early films were all made with fixed cameras. This greatly limited what could be achieved and made these early films more like the theatre than the modern cinema. So, an important improvement was the use of a moving camera, which could turn from side to side and also move about to follow the action. The Great Train Robbery was the first important experiment in the use of a moving camera. It was made in 1903 by Edwin Porter, an American, and lasted eight minutes. In the following years, films became much longer and the screens larger. Other changes were introduced too, but it was not until the early 1920's that an effective sound system was developed. Lee de Forest, another American, found a way of photographing the sound waves which accompanied the action. This solved the major problem of sound-picture synchronisation. A strange consequence of having sound was that, for a few years, the cameras were once again made a part of a complex device and this sound-proofing system was so large that it could not be moved about easily.

The last major change in the cinema was the development of colour. Coloured photography had been possible from the 1860's, but early films were normally black and white and any colouring was painted on by hand - an expensive, slow and not very effective technique. In 1922, the first real colour films were produced, using a two-colour system called Technicolor. In this system, they filmed whole sequences in one colour but the attempts to mix colours to get realistic effects were not very successful. In 1932, Technicolor was improved by the use of three main colours and the same system is used today. Colour took longer to be generally accepted than sound. It was expensive and people often felt that it was less realistic than black and white. This was partly, of course, because the quality was not always very high and so the pictures could look very strange. Since the 1930's, there have been many improvements in the techniques of the cinema, and the style of acting has changed a good deal. But after fifty years, the basics - moving pictures, colour and sound - are still the same.

task1.model_answer: Modern cinema evolved through several key technical breakthroughs from the 1890s to the 1930s. Initially, W.K.L. Dickson's Kinetoscope and the Lumiere brothers' Cinematographe were silent systems, though the latter introduced large-screen projection. Early films also relied on fixed cameras, making them resemble stage plays until Edwin Porter demonstrated the moving camera in 1903. In the early 1920s, Lee de Forest solved sound-picture synchronisation by photographing sound waves, even though bulky sound-proofing temporarily restricted camera movement. Finally, colour cinema progressed from slow hand-painting to two-colour Technicolor in 1922 and three-colour Technicolor in 1932, overcoming early scepticism about cost and realism.

task1.title: Summary: The Early Evolution of Cinema

task2.model_answer:
Throughout cinema history, new technologies have often faced resistance before becoming standard. As the passage shows, early audiences were slow to accept colour films because they were expensive and sometimes looked unnatural compared to black and white. Today, filmmakers and audiences debate innovations such as 3D projection, high frame rates, and artificial intelligence in much the same way.

In my view, technological advances generally improve filmmaking, provided they serve the story rather than overshadow it. Just as moving cameras and synchronised sound allowed directors to break away from static stage-like productions, modern digital effects and spatial audio help create immersive worlds that were once impossible to film. However, technical quality alone cannot rescue a weak script or unconvincing acting. When early three-colour Technicolor succeeded, it did so because its visual richness eventually enhanced realistic storytelling.

Ultimately, cinema thrives when technical innovation works hand in hand with strong artistic vision, turning new tools into lasting creative possibilities.

Sinema.

İlk hareketli görüntüler 1890'larda ABD'de çalışan bir İngiliz olan W. K. L. Dickson tarafından geliştirildi. Sistemine Kinetoskop adını verdi. Bu, bugün bildiğimiz anlamda sinema değildi. Görüntüler çok küçüktü ve aynı anda yalnızca bir kişi izleyebiliyordu. En eski Kinetoskop, bir fonografa (gramofon ve pikabın atası) ayrı olarak kaydedilmiş sesi kullanıyordu. Ancak görüntü ile sesi bir araya getirmede, yani senkronizasyonda birçok sorun vardı. Sonuç olarak, Kinetoskop sessiz biçimiyle yaygınlaştı. Aynı ilke Fransız Auguste ve Louis Lumiere tarafından geliştirildi. Sistemlerine Sinematograf adını verdiler ve 1895 ile 1900 yılları arasında bunu Avrupa'nın diğer bölgelerine, Hindistan'a, Avustralya'ya ve Japonya'ya ihraç etmeyi başardılar. Sinematograf büyük bir perde kullanıyordu, ancak filmler hâlâ çok kısaydı - yalnızca yaklaşık bir dakika uzunluğundaydı. Yaygınlaşan Kinetoskop gibi, bu da sessiz bir sistemdi.

İlk filmlerin tamamı sabit kameralarla çekiliyordu. Bu durum başarılabilecek şeyleri büyük ölçüde kısıtlıyor ve bu ilk filmleri modern sinemadan çok tiyatroya benzetiyordu. Bu nedenle önemli bir gelişme, bir yandan diğer yana dönebilen ve ayrıca hareketi takip etmek için etrafta dolaşabilen hareketli bir kameranın kullanılması oldu. The Great Train Robbery (Büyük Tren Soygunu), hareketli kamera kullanımındaki ilk önemli denemeydi. 1903 yılında Amerikalı Edwin Porter tarafından çekildi ve sekiz dakika sürdü. Sonraki yıllarda filmler çok daha uzun, perdeler ise daha büyük hâle geldi. Başka değişiklikler de getirildi, ancak etkili bir ses sisteminin geliştirilmesi 1920'lerin başlarına kadar gerçekleşmedi. Bir başka Amerikalı olan Lee de Forest, harekete eşlik eden ses dalgalarının fotoğrafını çekmenin bir yolunu buldu. Bu, ses ve görüntü senkronizasyonunun büyük sorununu çözdü. Sese sahip olmanın tuhaf bir sonucu olarak, birkaç yıl boyunca kameralar yeniden karmaşık bir cihazın parçası hâline getirildi ve bu ses yalıtım sistemi o kadar büyüktü ki kolayca hareket ettirilemiyordu.

Sinemadaki son büyük değişiklik rengin geliştirilmesiydi. Renkli fotoğrafçılık 1860'lardan itibaren mümkündü, ancak ilk filmler normalde siyah beyazdı ve herhangi bir renklendirme elle boyanarak yapılıyordu - pahalı, yavaş ve pek etkili olmayan bir teknik. 1922'de, Technicolor adı verilen iki renkli bir sistem kullanılarak ilk gerçek renkli filmler üretildi. Bu sistemde bütün sekanslar tek bir renkte çekiliyordu, ancak gerçekçi etkiler elde etmek için renkleri karıştırma girişimleri pek başarılı olmuyordu. 1932'de Technicolor üç ana rengin kullanılmasıyla geliştirildi ve bugün de aynı sistem kullanılmaktadır. Rengin genel olarak kabul görmesi sesten daha uzun sürdü. Pahalıydı ve insanlar genellikle siyah beyazdan daha az gerçekçi olduğunu hissediyordu. Elbette bunun bir nedeni, kalitenin her zaman çok yüksek olmaması ve bu yüzden görüntülerin çok tuhaf görünebilmesiydi. 1930'lardan bu yana sinema tekniklerinde birçok gelişme yaşandı ve oyunculuk tarzı da epey değişti. Ama elli yılın ardından temeller - hareketli görüntüler, renk ve ses - hâlâ aynıdır.

passages.passage_text:
The gorilla is something of a paradox in the African scene. One thinks one knows him very well. For a hundred years or more, he has been killed, captured, and imprisoned in zoos. His bones have been mounted in natural history museums everywhere, and he has always exerted a strong fascination upon scientists and romantics alike. He is the stereotyped monster of the horror films and the adventure books, and an obvious (though not perhaps strictly scientific) link with our ancestral past.

Yet, the fact is we know very little about gorillas. No really satisfactory photograph has ever been taken of one in a wild state, no zoologist, however intrepid, has been able to keep the animal under close and constant observation in the dark jungles in which he lives. Carl Akeley, the American naturalist, led two expeditions in the 1920's, and now lies buried among the animals he loved so much. But even he was unable to discover how long the gorilla lives, or how or why it dies; nor was he able to define the exact social pattern of the family groups, or indicate the final extent of their intelligence. All this and many other things remain almost as much a mystery as they were when the French explorer Du Chaillu first described the animal to the civilised world a century ago. The Abominable Snowman, who haunts the imagination of climbers in the Himalayas, is hardly more elusive.

task2.model_answer:
Many wild animals are kept in zoos and natural history museums, which raises an important debate about whether captivity is justified. On one hand, zoos allow people to see rare species such as gorillas up close and can spark public interest in wildlife conservation. Museums also preserve specimens that help educate students about biology and evolutionary history.

On the other hand, as the passage suggests, observing an animal in a cage reveals very little about its true nature. Deprived of its dark jungle habitat and complex family groups, a captive gorilla cannot display natural behavior. Moreover, capturing and imprisoning wild animals causes unnecessary stress and disrupts fragile populations.

In my opinion, studying animals in their natural habitats should take priority over keeping them in captivity. With modern non-invasive technology such as remote cameras, scientists can unlock the mysteries of elusive species without taking away their freedom.

passages.passage_text:
People have always wanted to know more about the other planets in our universe. Long ago, they found out that our earth is not flat but round, and that the moon goes round the sun. Telescopes were built to see planets far away in space better. But, of course, this was never enough. Men have always thought about visits to other planets and many people have written stories about journeys in space and what men hoped to find there. Often the ideas in these stories are strange and wrong. We know that now because real men have visited space and can tell us what life there is like.

The work of scientists in the last twenty years has shown the world that men can travel outside the earth's atmosphere in spaceships. These scientists all worked on the same idea: space travel. But it is sad that they did not work together. There were two teams who worked separately, one in the USSR and one in the USA. Many of them were Germans who left their country in 1945 after the Second World War. Wernher Von Braun, who worked for the USA, was the most famous one. They all tried to build rockets to go into space. Each of these countries wanted to be the first in space. So a race into space was started.

In 1957, the world outside the USSR learned a new word: 'sputnik'. This is the Russian word for a satellite, a planet which goes round and round another planet. A real satellite (like the moon, which is the earth's satellite) makes a circle round its planet, called an orbit. Sputnik 1, which was a small satellite, went into the earth's orbit and sent back radio signals. Then, after a month, Sputnik 2 followed. And this time, Laika, a dog, was aboard.

Then the USA came into the race. The first satellite they tried to send into space caught fire. The second, Explorer 1, went into orbit without any problems and sent back a lot of interesting information about the earth's atmosphere.

For a journey to the moon, scientists had to build new spaceships. These new spaceships, called 'probes', could move in space freely. Again the Americans tried several times, but could not launch their first moon probe. The Soviets also had problems with their probes, called Luniks. At last, Lunik 3 reached the moon and went into orbit round it. For the first time people on earth saw pictures of the other side of the moon.

In 1961, the Soviets were ready to take a risk. Yuri Gagarin flew into space. This 27-year-old Soviet was the first real spaceman. His spaceship made one orbit of the earth, and then landed safely. A few weeks later, the first American astronaut, Alan Shepard, followed him into space. Soon more Americans and more Soviets saw the world from space. They said it was very beautiful. Flights continued and men stayed in space longer and longer.

Finally, in 1969, after long preparations, the USA was ready for the longest space journey in all those years. Apollo 11 was sent to the moon with three astronauts. They brought back rock pieces and moon dust for the scientists to examine.

task1.model_answer: Space exploration moved from imagination to reality through rapid progress by competing teams in the USSR and the USA after World War II. In 1957, the Soviets launched the first satellites, Sputnik 1 and Sputnik 2, followed by the American satellite Explorer 1. Scientists later developed space probes, and Soviet Lunik 3 sent back the first images of the moon's far side. Human spaceflight began in 1961 with Yuri Gagarin and Alan Shepard. Finally, in 1969, the American Apollo 11 mission carried three astronauts to the moon and returned with lunar rocks and dust.
task1.prompt: Write a clear summary of the main stages in the space race described in the passage, from 1957 to 1969.
task1.title: Summary: Milestones of the Space Race

task2.model_answer:
During the space race described in the passage, the USSR and the USA worked separately because each country wanted to be first. Although this competition pushed technology forward quickly, I believe international cooperation is a much better approach to space exploration.

First, building rockets, probes, and spaceships is extremely expensive. When nations share the costs and combine their best scientists, they can achieve bigger goals without wasting money on repeating the same work. Second, sharing scientific data and technology reduces the risk of accidents and speeds up discoveries that benefit everyone on Earth, such as improved communications and climate monitoring.

In conclusion, while rivalry once motivated rapid progress, modern space exploration is safer, cheaper, and more effective when countries work together as a single team.
task2.prompt: In the passage, the author writes that it was sad scientists in the USSR and the USA did not work together. Do you think countries should cooperate rather than compete in space exploration? Give reasons for your opinion.
task2.title: Opinion Paragraph: Cooperation vs. Competition in Space

passages.tts_script_tr:
Uzay Yolculuğu.

İnsanlar evrenimizdeki diğer gezegenler hakkında her zaman daha fazla şey öğrenmek istemişlerdir. Uzun zaman önce, dünyamızın düz değil yuvarlak olduğunu ve ayın güneşin etrafında döndüğünü keşfettiler. Uzaydaki uzak gezegenleri daha iyi görmek için teleskoplar yapıldı. Ama elbette bu hiçbir zaman yeterli olmadı. İnsanlar her zaman başka gezegenlere yapılan ziyaretleri düşündüler ve birçok kişi uzay yolculukları ile insanların orada bulmayı umduğu şeyler hakkında hikâyeler yazdı. Bu hikâyelerdeki fikirler çoğu zaman tuhaf ve yanlıştır. Bunu artık biliyoruz çünkü gerçek insanlar uzayı ziyaret etti ve bize oradaki yaşamın nasıl olduğunu anlatabiliyor.

Bilim insanlarının son yirmi yıldaki çalışmaları, insanlığın uzay gemileriyle dünya atmosferinin dışına çıkabileceğini tüm dünyaya göstermiştir. Bu bilim insanlarının hepsi aynı fikir üzerinde çalıştı: uzay yolculuğu. Ancak birlikte çalışmamış olmaları üzücüdür. Biri SSCB'de, diğeri ABD'de olmak üzere ayrı ayrı çalışan iki ekip vardı. Bunların çoğu, 1945'te İkinci Dünya Savaşı'ndan sonra ülkelerinden ayrılan Almanlardı. ABD için çalışan Wernher Von Braun en ünlüleriydi. Hepsi uzaya gitmek için roketler inşa etmeye çalıştı. Bu ülkelerin her biri uzaya çıkan ilk ülke olmak istiyordu. Böylece bir uzay yarışı başladı.

1957'de SSCB dışındaki dünya yeni bir kelime öğrendi: 'sputnik'. Bu, bir başka gezegenin etrafında dönüp duran bir gezegen olan uydu anlamındaki Rusça kelimedir. Gerçek bir uydu (dünyanın uydusu olan ay gibi), gezegeninin etrafında yörünge adı verilen bir daire çizer. Küçük bir uydu olan Sputnik 1, dünyanın yörüngesine girdi ve geri radyo sinyalleri gönderdi. Ardından bir ay sonra Sputnik 2 onu takip etti. Ve bu kez araçta Laika adında bir köpek vardı.

Ardından ABD yarışa katıldı. Uzaya göndermeye çalıştıkları ilk uydu alev aldı. İkincisi olan Explorer 1 ise hiçbir sorun yaşamadan yörüngeye oturdu ve dünyanın atmosferi hakkında pek çok ilginç bilgi gönderdi.

Ay'a yapılacak bir yolculuk için bilim insanlarının yeni uzay gemileri inşa etmesi gerekiyordu. 'Sonda' adı verilen bu yeni uzay gemileri uzayda serbestçe hareket edebiliyordu. Amerikalılar yine birkaç kez denedi, ancak ilk ay sondalarını fırlatamadılar. Sovyetler de Lunik adı verilen sondalarıyla sorunlar yaşadı. Nihayet Lunik 3 Ay'a ulaştı ve etrafında yörüngeye girdi. Dünyadaki insanlar ilk kez Ay'ın diğer tarafının fotoğraflarını gördü.

1961'de Sovyetler bir risk almaya hazırdı. Yuri Gagarin uzaya uçtu. Bu 27 yaşındaki Sovyet vatandaşı ilk gerçek uzay adamıydı. Uzay gemisi dünyanın etrafında bir tur attı ve ardından güvenli bir şekilde iniş yaptı. Birkaç hafta sonra ilk Amerikalı astronot Alan Shepard onu uzaya takip etti. Kısa süre içinde daha fazla Amerikalı ve daha fazla Sovyet dünyayı uzaydan gördü. Çok güzel olduğunu söylediler. Uçuşlar devam etti ve insanlar uzayda giderek daha uzun süre kaldı.

Sonunda, 1969'da, uzun hazırlıkların ardından ABD, tüm o yıllardaki en uzun uzay yolculuğuna hazırdı. Apollo 11 üç astronotla Ay'a gönderildi. Bilim insanlarının incelemesi için kaya parçaları ve ay tozu geri getirdiler.

passages.passage_text:
Petroleum, or oil, is the world's most important source of energy. It is produced in more than sixty countries throughout the world, but there are mainly six important petroleum producing regions in the world. The problem is: how can we determine the possible regions for oil? Drilling a well is a difficult and expensive operation. Therefore, an oil company first looks for good indications, or signs, of oil in an area. The aim of this exploration is to discover the best areas for drilling.

There are four stages in the process of exploration: aerial surveys, a geological survey, a geophysical survey and exploration drilling.

In an aerial survey, a survey of the area is made from an aeroplane. There are two different types of aerial survey: the photographic and the magnetic. During the former, photographs are taken from an aeroplane, showing the most important geological features on the earth's surface. Maps are made from these photographs. During the magnetic survey, the earth's magnetism is recorded. Rock formations under the earth's surface differ from place to place. As a result, the intensity of the earth's magnetism and the thickness of the rocks are not the same everywhere. The measurements are analysed and in this way information is obtained about the rock formations. The geologists then look for signs of oil in these formations. If the indications are good, exploration continues.

A geological survey is the next stage. Certain rock formations are visited. By examining these structures, geologists learn about the shape and direction of the rock formations under the surface. Samples of rock are taken to the laboratory and analysed. If the samples contain fossils, these will indicate the age of the rock. Fossils of marine animals show that there may be oil in the area.

Geophysical surveys are used to confirm the results of geological surveys. During a geophysical survey, an explosion is made on the earth's surface. The rocks under the earth vibrate. These vibrations, called seismic waves, travel down into the earth. Some of them, however, are reflected by rock layers under the surface and 'heard' by special equipment. The waves are recorded on a seismogram. Analysis of this information shows the depth and type of rock formations.

All these surveys can help to locate structures under the earth's surface. But still there may be no oil. There is only one way to be sure, and that is to drill a well. The first wells are called exploration wells or wildcats. A wildcat without any oil is called a dry hole. A discovery well is wildcat with some oil. When oil is discovered, several more wells are drilled in the same field. These are known as production wells.

Exploration for oil is a long, difficult and expensive process. However, it reduces drilling, which saves money.

task1.model_answer: Oil companies conduct a four-stage exploration process to locate promising drilling sites and avoid unnecessary expenses. First, aerial surveys use photographs to map surface features and magnetic measurements to study underground rock thickness. Second, in a geological survey, geologists inspect rock formations, analyse samples in a laboratory, and look for marine fossils that suggest oil may exist. Third, geophysical surveys use surface explosions to send seismic waves underground, which are recorded on a seismogram to reveal rock depth and type. Finally, exploration drilling confirms whether oil is actually present; successful discovery wells are followed by production wells.
task1.prompt: Summarize the four stages of oil exploration and explain why companies follow this process before full production drilling.
task1.title: Summary: The Four Stages of Oil Exploration

task2.model_answer:
Petroleum remains the world's most important energy source, yet finding and extracting it is both costly and environmentally sensitive. Some people argue that countries should continue investing heavily in oil exploration to maintain economic stability, while others believe resources should shift rapidly toward renewable energy.

Proponents of continued exploration point out that modern industries, transport, and heating still depend heavily on oil. Without discovering new reserves, energy prices could rise sharply and harm developing economies. Moreover, careful geological and geophysical surveys reduce unnecessary drilling, limiting surface disruption.

However, relying solely on fossil fuels carries serious long-term risks, including pollution and climate change. Even with advanced exploration methods, drilling remains expensive and uncertain.

In my view, oil exploration should continue only as a temporary bridge while governments invest aggressively in solar, wind, and clean technologies. Balancing current energy needs with a steady transition to renewables is the most responsible strategy for the future.
task2.prompt: Although oil exploration is expensive and difficult, petroleum remains the world's most important source of energy. Should countries continue investing in searching for new oil reserves, or focus entirely on renewable energy? Discuss both sides and state your opinion.
task2.title: Opinion Essay: Investing in Oil Exploration vs. Renewable Energy

passages.tts_script_tr:
Petrol Arama.

Ham petrol ya da petrol, dünyanın en önemli enerji kaynağıdır. Dünya genelinde altmıştan fazla ülkede üretilmektedir, ancak dünyada başlıca altı önemli petrol üretim bölgesi vardır. Sorun şudur: Olası petrol bölgelerini nasıl belirleyebiliriz? Kuyu açmak zor ve pahalı bir işlemdir. Bu nedenle bir petrol şirketi önce bir bölgede petrole dair iyi belirtiler ya da işaretler arar. Bu aramanın amacı sondaj için en iyi alanları keşfetmektir.

Arama sürecinde dört aşama vardır: havadan etütler, jeolojik etüt, jeofizik etüt ve arama sondajı.

Havadan etütte, bölgenin incelemesi bir uçaktan yapılır. İki farklı havadan etüt türü vardır: fotoğrafik ve manyetik. İlkinde, uçaktan yeryüzündeki en önemli jeolojik özellikleri gösteren fotoğraflar çekilir. Bu fotoğraflardan haritalar çıkarılır. Manyetik etüt sırasında ise dünyanın manyetizması kaydedilir. Yeryüzünün altındaki kaya oluşumları yerden yere farklılık gösterir. Sonuç olarak, dünyanın manyetizmasının şiddeti ve kayaların kalınlığı her yerde aynı değildir. Ölçümler analiz edilir ve bu şekilde kaya oluşumları hakkında bilgi elde edilir. Jeologlar daha sonra bu oluşumlarda petrol izleri arar. Belirtiler iyiyse arama devam eder.

Bir sonraki aşama jeolojik etüttür. Belirli kaya oluşumları ziyaret edilir. Jeologlar bu yapıları inceleyerek yer altındaki kaya oluşumlarının şekli ve yönü hakkında bilgi edinirler. Kaya örnekleri laboratuvara götürülür ve analiz edilir. Örnekler fosil içeriyorsa, bunlar kayanın yaşını gösterir. Deniz canlılarının fosilleri bölgede petrol olabileceğini gösterir.

Jeofizik etütler, jeolojik etütlerin sonuçlarını doğrulamak için kullanılır. Jeofizik etüt sırasında yeryüzünde bir patlama gerçekleştirilir. Yer altındaki kayalar titreşir. Sismik dalgalar adı verilen bu titreşimler yerin derinliklerine doğru ilerler. Ancak bunların bir kısmı yer altındaki kaya katmanları tarafından yansıtılır ve özel ekipmanlar tarafından 'duyulur'. Dalgalar bir sismogram üzerine kaydedilir. Bu bilgilerin analizi, kaya oluşumlarının derinliğini ve türünü gösterir.

Tüm bu etütler yer altındaki yapıların yerini belirlemeye yardımcı olabilir. Ancak yine de petrol olmayabilir. Emin olmanın tek bir yolu vardır, o da kuyu açmaktır. İlk kuyulara arama kuyuları veya 'wildcat' (deneme kuyusu) denir. İçinde hiç petrol bulunmayan bir deneme kuyusu kuru kuyu olarak adlandırılır. Keşif kuyusu ise içinde bir miktar petrol bulunan bir deneme kuyusudur. Petrol keşfedildiğinde aynı sahada birkaç kuyu daha açılır. Bunlar üretim kuyuları olarak bilinir.

Petrol arama uzun, zor ve pahalı bir süreçtir. Ancak sondajı azaltır, bu da para tasarrufu sağlar.

passages.passage_text:
With a tremendous roar from its rocket engine, the satellite is sent up into the sky. Minutes later, at an altitude of 300 miles, this tiny electronic moon begins to orbit the earth. Its radio begins to transmit a staggering amount of information about the satellite's orbital path, the amount of radiation it detects, and the presence of meteorites. Information of all kinds races back to the earth. No human being could possibly copy down all these facts, much less remember and organize them. But an electronic computer can.

The marvel of the machine age, the electronic computer, has been in use only since 1946. It can do simple computations - add, subtract, multiply, and divide - with lightning speed and perfect accuracy. It can multiply two 10-digit numbers in 1/1,000 second, a problem that would take an average person five minutes to do with pencil and paper. Some computers can work 500,000 times faster than any person can.

Once it is given a 'program'; that is, a carefully worked-out set of instructions devised by a technician trained in computer language, a computer can gather a wide range of information for many purposes. For the scientist, it can get information from outer space or from the depths of the ocean. In business and industry, the computer prepares factory inventories, keeps track of sales trends and production needs, mails dividend checks, and makes out company payrolls. It can keep bank accounts up to date and make out electric bills. If you are planning a trip by plane, the computer will find out what route to take and what space is available.

Not only can the computer gather facts, it can also store them as fast as they are gathered and can pour them out whenever they are needed. The computer is really a high-powered 'memory' machine that "has all the answers" - or almost all. What is the most efficient speed for driving a car through the New York-New Jersey tunnels? What brand of canned goods is the most popular in a particular supermarket? What kind of weather will we have tomorrow? The computer will flash out the answers in a fraction of a second.

Besides gathering and storing information, the computer can also solve complicated problems that once took months for people to do. For example, within sixteen hours an electronic brain named CHEOPS (which stands for Chemical Engineering Optimization System) solved a difficult design problem. First, it was fed all the information necessary for designing a chemical plant. After running through 16,000 possible designs, it picked out the plan for the plant that would produce the most chemical at the lowest cost. Then, it issued a printed set of exact specifications. Before CHEOPS solved this problem, a team of engineers having the same information had worked for a year to produce only three designs, none of which was as efficient as the computer's.

At times computers seem almost human. They can 'read' handprinted letters, play chess, compose music, write plays, and even design other computers. Is it any wonder that they are sometimes called 'thinking' machines?

Not even computers can predict the future, but the benefits of computers are becoming more obvious every day.

a) Computers are being used in space travel. Rockets, satellites and spaceships are guided by computers.

b) Computers are being used in aviation. They are used in the training of airline pilots. Computers also direct the flight of planes from one city to another, control their air speeds and altitudes, and even land them.

c) Computers are being used in medicine. They are used in analyzing blood samples, in diagnosing disease, and in prescribing medication. They also keep records of the tissue types of patients waiting for organ transplants.

Even though they are taking over some of the tasks that were once accomplished by our own brains, computers are not replacing us - at least not yet. Our brain has more than 10 billion cells. A computer has only a few hundred thousand parts. For some time to come, then, we can safely say that our brains are at least 10,000 times more complex than a computer. How we use them is for us, not the computer, to decide.

passages.title: The Computer
passages.tts_script:
The Computer.

With a tremendous roar from its rocket engine, the satellite is sent up into the sky. Minutes later, at an altitude of 300 miles, this tiny electronic moon begins to orbit the earth. Its radio begins to transmit a staggering amount of information about the satellite's orbital path, the amount of radiation it detects, and the presence of meteorites. Information of all kinds races back to the earth. No human being could possibly copy down all these facts, much less remember and organize them. But an electronic computer can.

The marvel of the machine age, the electronic computer, has been in use only since 1946. It can do simple computations, add, subtract, multiply, and divide, with lightning speed and perfect accuracy. It can multiply two 10-digit numbers in one thousandth of a second, a problem that would take an average person five minutes to do with pencil and paper. Some computers can work 500,000 times faster than any person can.

Once it is given a program, that is, a carefully worked-out set of instructions devised by a technician trained in computer language, a computer can gather a wide range of information for many purposes. For the scientist, it can get information from outer space or from the depths of the ocean. In business and industry, the computer prepares factory inventories, keeps track of sales trends and production needs, mails dividend checks, and makes out company payrolls. It can keep bank accounts up to date and make out electric bills. If you are planning a trip by plane, the computer will find out what route to take and what space is available.

Not only can the computer gather facts, it can also store them as fast as they are gathered and can pour them out whenever they are needed. The computer is really a high-powered memory machine that "has all the answers," or almost all. What is the most efficient speed for driving a car through the New York to New Jersey tunnels? What brand of canned goods is the most popular in a particular supermarket? What kind of weather will we have tomorrow? The computer will flash out the answers in a fraction of a second.

Besides gathering and storing information, the computer can also solve complicated problems that once took months for people to do. For example, within sixteen hours an electronic brain named CHEOPS, which stands for Chemical Engineering Optimization System, solved a difficult design problem. First, it was fed all the information necessary for designing a chemical plant. After running through 16,000 possible designs, it picked out the plan for the plant that would produce the most chemical at the lowest cost. Then, it issued a printed set of exact specifications. Before CHEOPS solved this problem, a team of engineers having the same information had worked for a year to produce only three designs, none of which was as efficient as the computer's.

At times computers seem almost human. They can read handprinted letters, play chess, compose music, write plays, and even design other computers. Is it any wonder that they are sometimes called thinking machines?

Not even computers can predict the future, but the benefits of computers are becoming more obvious every day.

First, computers are being used in space travel. Rockets, satellites, and spaceships are guided by computers.

Second, computers are being used in aviation. They are used in the training of airline pilots. Computers also direct the flight of planes from one city to another, control their air speeds and altitudes, and even land them.

Third, computers are being used in medicine. They are used in analyzing blood samples, in diagnosing disease, and in prescribing medication. They also keep records of the tissue types of patients waiting for organ transplants.

Even though they are taking over some of the tasks that were once accomplished by our own brains, computers are not replacing us, at least not yet. Our brain has more than 10 billion cells. A computer has only a few hundred thousand parts. For some time to come, then, we can safely say that our brains are at least 10,000 times more complex than a computer. How we use them is for us, not the computer, to decide.

task1.model_answer: Electronic computers have transformed how information is gathered, stored, and processed since 1946. Operating far faster and more accurately than humans, computers follow programmed instructions to serve scientists, businesses, and travelers by managing data, inventories, payrolls, and flight bookings. Beyond storing facts, they solve complex engineering problems rapidly, as seen when CHEOPS evaluated 16,000 chemical plant designs in sixteen hours. Today, computers guide spacecraft, assist in pilot training and air traffic control, and support doctors in diagnosis and treatment. Nevertheless, human brains remain vastly more complex and continue to direct how computers are used.

task2.model_answer:
Although computers perform calculations and manage massive datasets far faster than humans, they are unlikely to replace human intelligence completely. Computers excel at repetitive, rule-based tasks such as analyzing medical data, guiding aircraft, and optimizing industrial designs. By handling these demanding computations quickly and accurately, machines free people from tedious work and reduce human error in critical fields like aviation and healthcare.

However, human thinking involves far more than processing speed. Creativity, ethical judgment, empathy, and the ability to adapt to unfamiliar situations remain uniquely human strengths. As the passage highlights, the human brain contains billions of cells and is thousands of times more complex than a machine. Moreover, computers cannot set their own goals or take responsibility for moral decisions; they rely on human programmers and operators to define their purpose. Therefore, rather than replacing us, computers are most valuable as powerful tools that extend human capability under our guidance.

passages.tts_script_tr:
Bilgisayar.

Roket motorunun muazzam gürültüsüyle uydu gökyüzüne fırlatılır. Dakikalar sonra, 300 mil yükseklikte bu minik elektronik ay Dünya'nın yörüngesinde dönmeye başlar. Telsizi; uydunun yörünge yolu, tespit ettiği radyasyon miktarı ve göktaşlarının varlığı hakkında baş döndürücü miktarda bilgi iletmeye başlar. Her türden bilgi hızla Dünya'ya ulaşır. Hiçbir insan bütün bu verileri yazıya dökemez, kaldı ki hatırlayıp düzenleyemez. Ama bir elektronik bilgisayar bunu yapabilir.

Makine çağının harikası olan elektronik bilgisayar, yalnızca 1946'dan beri kullanılmaktadır. Toplama, çıkarma, çarpma ve bölme gibi basit hesaplamaları yıldırım hızıyla ve kusursuz bir doğrulukla yapabilir. Ortalama bir insanın kâğıt kalemle beş dakikada çözebileceği iki 10 basamaklı sayıyı çarpma işlemini saniyenin binde birinde gerçekleştirebilir. Bazı bilgisayarlar herhangi bir insandan 500.000 kat daha hızlı çalışabilir.

Bilgisayar dilinde eğitim almış bir teknisyen tarafından hazırlanan, yani özenle oluşturulmuş bir talimatlar bütünü olan bir program verildiğinde, bilgisayar pek çok amaç için çok geniş bir yelpazede bilgi toplayabilir. Bilim insanları için uzaydan ya da okyanusların derinliklerinden bilgi elde edebilir. İş dünyasında ve sanayide bilgisayar; fabrika envanterlerini hazırlar, satış eğilimlerini ve üretim ihtiyaçlarını takip eder, temettü çeklerini postalar ve şirket maaş bordrolarını düzenler. Banka hesaplarını güncel tutabilir ve elektrik faturalarını çıkarabilir. Uçakla bir seyahat planlıyorsanız, hangi rotayı izleyeceğinizi ve hangi yerlerin müsait olduğunu bilgisayar bulur.

Bilgisayar yalnızca bilgileri toplamakla kalmaz, aynı zamanda onları toplandığı hızla depolayabilir ve ihtiyaç duyulduğu her an dışarı aktarabilir. Bilgisayar gerçekten de "tüm cevaplara" ya da neredeyse tümüne sahip yüksek güçlü bir hafıza makinesidir. New York'tan New Jersey'ye uzanan tünellerden araç sürerken en verimli hız nedir? Belirli bir süpermarkette hangi konserve markası en popülerdir? Yarın nasıl bir hava durumu olacak? Bilgisayar cevapları saniyenin çok küçük bir kesrinde ekrana yansıtır.

Bilgisayar, bilgi toplamanın ve depolamanın yanı sıra bir zamanlar insanların yapmasının aylar sürdüğü karmaşık problemleri de çözebilir. Örneğin, açılımı Kimya Mühendisliği Optimizasyon Sistemi olan CHEOPS adlı bir elektronik beyin, zorlu bir tasarım problemini on altı saat içinde çözdü. İlk olarak kendisine bir kimya tesisi tasarlamak için gerekli tüm bilgiler yüklendi. Olası 16.000 tasarımı inceledikten sonra, en düşük maliyetle en fazla kimyasalı üretecek tesis planını seçti. Ardından kesin teknik özelliklerin basılı bir dökümünü verdi. CHEOPS bu problemi çözmeden önce, aynı bilgilere sahip bir mühendis ekibi yalnızca üç tasarım üretebilmek için bir yıl boyunca çalışmıştı ve bunların hiçbiri bilgisayarınki kadar verimli değildi.

Bilgisayarlar zaman zaman neredeyse insan gibi görünür. El yazısıyla yazılmış harfleri okuyabilir, satranç oynayabilir, müzik besteleyebilir, oyun yazabilir ve hatta başka bilgisayarlar tasarlayabilirler. Bazen düşünen makineler olarak adlandırılmalarına şaşırmamak mümkün mü?

Bilgisayarlar bile geleceği tahmin edemez ama bilgisayarların faydaları her geçen gün daha da belirgin hale gelmektedir.

İlk olarak, bilgisayarlar uzay yolculuğunda kullanılmaktadır. Roketler, uydular ve uzay gemileri bilgisayarlar tarafından yönlendirilir.

İkinci olarak, bilgisayarlar havacılıkta kullanılmaktadır. Havayolu pilotlarının eğitiminde kullanılırlar. Bilgisayarlar ayrıca uçakların bir şehirden diğerine uçuşunu yönlendirir, hava hızlarını ve irtifalarını kontrol eder, hatta onları indirir.

Üçüncü olarak, bilgisayarlar tıpta kullanılmaktadır. Kan örneklerinin analizinde, hastalıkların teşhisinde ve ilaç yazılmasında kullanılırlar. Ayrıca organ nakli bekleyen hastaların doku tiplerinin kayıtlarını da tutarlar.

Bir zamanlar kendi beyinlerimiz tarafından yerine getirilen görevlerin bazılarını devralıyor olsalar da bilgisayarlar yerimizi almıyor, en azından henüz. Beynimizde 10 milyardan fazla hücre vardır. Bir bilgisayarın ise yalnızca birkaç yüz bin parçası bulunur. Öyleyse önümüzdeki uzun bir süre boyunca, beyinlerimizin bir bilgisayardan en az 10.000 kat daha karmaşık olduğunu güvenle söyleyebiliriz. Onları nasıl kullanacağımıza bilgisayar değil, biz karar vereceğiz.

passages.passage_text:
At one time, students used to be told: "We don't know what electricity is, we don't know how electricity goes through a solid wire," etc. The electron theory explains these things clearly and simply. In addition, it explains the true meaning of voltage, resistance, etc. Therefore, an understanding of the electron theory is basic to the understanding of the electrical and electronic theory.

Scientists now agree that our universe is basically dependent on two factors, one of which is matter, the other, energy. Matter is anything that occupies space and has weight. It can exist in any of the three forms: solid, liquid or gas.

Matter is composed of protons, neutrons and electrons. The proton has a positive charge. This component has very little weight. The neutron has no charge, but it supplies almost all the weight of matter. The electron has a negative charge. It also has very little weight. If we could look at the structure of a piece of copper, we would find that it consists of a specific number of protons, neutrons, and electrons arranged in some particular way. In a piece of iron, a certain number of protons, neutrons, and electrons are arranged in a different way. The proton of iron is identical to that of copper and other elements. They are all made up of the same components. It is the arrangement of these components that makes them different.

The electrons of an atom are arranged in shells around the nucleus. The electrons in the last shell are called 'valence' electrons and the electrical properties of a material are dependent on the number of such electrons. Atoms with less than four valence electrons give up one or more electrons, and the fewer the valence electrons, the easier this becomes. Atoms with more than 4 electrons in their last shell take one or more additional electrons. The conduction of electricity is made possible by the free electrons in the outer shell.

Metals are good conductors of electricity as they have less than 4 valence electrons. These electrons aren't strongly attached to the nucleus, but the ones in the inner shell are. Therefore, in a metal, they can move easily from one nucleus to another.

task1.model_answer: The electron theory provides a clear foundation for understanding electricity, voltage, and resistance. In our universe, matter is composed of three basic particles: positively charged protons, uncharged neutrons that supply nearly all the weight, and negatively charged electrons. Different elements such as copper and iron share these exact same components, differing only in how they are arranged. Electrons orbit the nucleus in shells, and those in the outermost shell—called valence electrons—determine a material's electrical behavior. task2.model_answer:
Understanding basic scientific theories, such as the electron theory, is essential even for everyday life in a modern technological society. Almost every activity people rely on today—from lighting homes and charging phones to running hospitals and transportation networks—depends on electrical and electronic systems. Without a basic grasp of how electricity moves through conductors, individuals cannot fully understand how everyday devices function or why safety rules around electrical equipment matter.

Furthermore, scientific literacy helps people make informed decisions in a rapidly changing world. As societies transition toward renewable energy, electric vehicles, and advanced electronics, citizens and workers alike benefit from knowing the fundamental principles behind these technologies. Even students who do not pursue engineering or physics careers gain critical-thinking skills by learning how invisible phenomena like electric current follow simple, logical rules. In short, foundational scientific knowledge empowers people to use technology safely, responsibly, and intelligently.
